whyThisMatters: Real payment decisions are fast — an invoice lands, a deadline looms, and you don't always get time to research whether a request is safe. This game trains your reflex for good habits, and helps you catch things that only sound safe.
rememberThis: This month's habit to carry forward: fast instinct is good, but some things only sound safe — a matching PO number, a reply that confirms an address is active, a confident senior name. When you are not sure, slow down and check before you trust the label.

discussionPrompts: Ask the group which bubble tricked them. Most people get at least one of the trick bubbles wrong on their first try.
Ask why "Checked PO Reference Number" still only counts as a partial check, even though it's a real and useful habit.
Ask why replying to an email to confirm a bank change feels like verification but isn't.
facilitatorNotes.commonWrongAnswer: The most common mistake is tapping anything that sounds like a check — like a matching PO number, a reply confirming receipt, or a number printed in the email itself — without realising none of these actually verify who is asking. The trick bubbles are there to catch that habit.

bubbles.text: Updated Bank Details From Email Alone
Wired Funds To New Account Same Day

bubbles.note: A second approver is a real, strong control — but only if that person actually checks the bank details independently, rather than approving on trust because a colleague already signed off.

Matching the PO number is a genuinely useful first check, but it only confirms the invoice matches a real job — it does not by itself prove the bank details are genuine, since attackers can include a real PO number too.

bubbles.text: Called The Number In The Email
bubbles.note: Calling back feels like verification, but a number supplied in the suspicious email itself may ring the attacker directly — only a number you already had before this request counts.
Replying to the same email only confirms the address is active — it never proves who is actually behind it.
